bath.intro: Bath's oldest trees are yews planted in the 1730s for Prior Park, the garden Ralph Allen built above the city with Alexander Pope. The rest stand in the Georgian city itself. There are five planes in the Circus planted against carriage dust, a giant plane at Abbey Green, a lone survivor elm in Royal Victoria Park, and in Sydney Gardens a plane thought to be older than the gardens, a beech that may once have been a hedge, a sequoia beside the railway and a yellow bean tree the gardens list as the tallest in Britain and Ireland.
bath.meta_description: Nine remarkable trees in Bath: Prior Park's 1730s yews, the Circus planes, Abbey Green's giant plane and a Sydney Gardens plane thought to date from 1777.
bath.question_meta: The yews near Prior Park's Sham Bridge are Bath's oldest confirmed trees, planted in the 1730s in Ralph Allen and Alexander Pope's original garden.
bath.question_answer: Bath's oldest confirmed trees are the yews near Prior Park's Sham Bridge, planted as part of Ralph Allen and Alexander Pope's original 18th-century landscape garden, roughly 280 to 296 years old. They stand inside the National Trust's Prior Park Landscape Garden, a 25 minute walk from Bath Spa railway station, with a paid admission.
bath.question_context: Ralph Allen, the postal reformer and quarry owner who financed much of Georgian Bath, began building Prior Park on the hillside above the city in the 1730s, working with the poet Alexander Pope and, later, Capability Brown. A group of yews along the path east of the Sham Bridge, a stone crossing built to look ruined, dates to that original design rather than any Victorian replanting. A second band marks the woodland's northern edge near the dam between the middle and northern ponds. In winter hawfinches, a shy finch rarely seen in Britain, feed on their seeds. The nearest rival is free to see. The great plane in Sydney Gardens, 6.6 metres round, is thought by the gardens' own tree trail to have been planted in 1777, eighteen years before the gardens opened, which would make it around 250 years old. The trail says "thought to", so the yews keep the title. In the city centre, the plane at Abbey Green is tied by tradition to 1793, though map evidence suggests a planting closer to the 1880s.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Bath?
faq.a: A group of yews near the Sham Bridge in Prior Park Landscape Garden, planted in the 1730s as part of Ralph Allen and Alexander Pope's original design for the garden, making them roughly 280 to 296 years old.

faq.q: What old trees are in Sydney Gardens?
faq.a: A London plane 6.6 metres round that the gardens' tree trail thinks was planted in 1777, before the gardens opened in 1795; a 30-metre beech near the Sydney Road gate; a giant sequoia beside the railway; and a yellow bean tree in front of the Temple of Minerva that the trail lists as the tallest of its kind in Britain and Ireland. The park is free and open all year.

faq.q: What is the plane tree at Abbey Green in Bath?
faq.a: A giant London Plane at the centre of Abbey Green, a small square just south of Bath Abbey. Local tradition dates it to 1793, though map evidence suggests the tree visible today may date closer to the 1880s; either way it has stood over the square for well over a century.

faq.q: Are the trees in the Circus in Bath free to see?
faq.a: Yes. The Circus's central green is a public space, and its five London Plane trees, planted by residents around 1820 to cut down on dust from horse-drawn carriages, can be seen at any time at no charge.

faq.q: Is Prior Park Landscape Garden free to visit?
faq.a: No, Prior Park is a National Trust property with paid admission, though National Trust members enter free. Hours change with the season, so check the National Trust page before you go.

bristol.intro: Five of Bristol's remarkable trees stand on one walk of about two kilometres through the centre, from the planes of Queen Square to a fig growing out of the harbour wall and a cedar 5.95 metres round in Clifton. The oldest stand further out, in the estates and woods the city inherited: Ashton Court's Domesday Oak, around 700 years old, a sessile oak at Bishops Knoll that may be six trees fused into one, a yew swallowing a parish wall in Leigh Woods and a hollow plane bricked up against fires in Nightingale Valley. Twenty-two trees in all.
bristol.meta_description: Twenty-two remarkable trees in Bristol, from Queen Square's planes to Ashton Court's 700-year-old Domesday Oak and a yew swallowing a Leigh Woods wall.
bristol.question_meta: The Domesday Oak in Ashton Court, around 700 years old, is Bristol's oldest tree, still alive despite a partly collapsed, wire-supported trunk.
bristol.question_answer: Bristol's oldest tree is the Domesday Oak in Ashton Court Estate, estimated at around 700 years old and named for the estate's mention in the 1086 Domesday Book. Its trunk has partially collapsed and is now held together with timber struts and wire, but it is still alive, one of Britain's 50 Great Trees named by the Tree Council in 2002. It stands free to visit in Ashton Court, a short bus ride from central Bristol.
bristol.question_context: Ashton Court was a private deer park for centuries before Bristol City Council bought it in 1959 and opened it to the public. Its oldest surviving oak takes its name from the estate's appearance in the Domesday Book of 1086, and in 2002 the Tree Council chose it as one of 50 Great British Trees. Its trunk has since split and settled toward the ground and is held up with timber struts and steel wire, but it still comes into leaf each year. Every age in this contest is an estimate, and the nearest rival is close. Across the city in Bishops Knoll Wood, a sessile oak seven metres round is put at up to 600 years by the Woodland Trust, which owns the wood, and at 700 by the Bristol Tree Forum, possibly a bundle of young oaks planted together and fused. Leigh Woods adds a yew the National Trust puts at about 500 years, growing in a gap in an old parish wall. In the city centre, the oldest on record is the oak on Brandon Hill, around 300 years.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Bristol?
faq.a: The Domesday Oak in Ashton Court, around 700 years old and named for the estate's mention in the 1086 Domesday Book. Its trunk has partly collapsed and is held up with struts and wire, but it is still alive. A sessile oak in Bishops Knoll Wood is estimated at 600 to 700 years, so the two are close.

faq.q: Where can I see old trees in central Bristol?
faq.a: On foot in an afternoon. Start at the London Planes of Queen Square, then the fig growing out of the harbour wall east of Bristol Bridge, the city's largest black mulberry in Royal Fort Gardens, the oak on Brandon Hill and the cedar in Victoria Square, Clifton, about two kilometres in all and free throughout.

faq.q: Is Ashton Court free to visit?
faq.a: Yes. Ashton Court Estate is owned and managed by Bristol City Council and is open daily from 8am at no charge, though a small car parking fee applies for drivers.

faq.q: What trees are at Blaise Castle Estate?
faq.a: Cedars of Lebanon, an Atlas cedar and a holm oak stand among the specimen trees Humphry Repton planted for the estate in the late 1790s. Older than all of them is a sweet chestnut seven metres round in the meadow off Henbury Road, which the Bristol Tree Forum puts at about 550 years, and two Wellingtonias stand by the lower pond in Combe Dingle. The grounds are a free public park.

faq.q: Which old trees in Bristol are in woods rather than parks?
faq.a: Leigh Woods, across the Clifton Suspension Bridge, has a yew of about 500 years growing in a gap in an old parish wall. Bishops Knoll Wood in Stoke Bishop has a sessile oak of 600 to 700 years and a Monterey cypress still inside its Victorian railings. Hermitage Wood in Stoke Park has three veteran horse chestnuts. All are free and open.

faq.q: How old are the trees in Queen Square, Bristol?
faq.a: The London Planes around Queen Square's edge date to roughly the 1880s, making them around 145 years old. They replaced earlier avenue plantings from 1716, part of a square that has stood since 1699.

glastonbury.intro: Glastonbury's three trees cover a span no record can measure. Magog, east of the Tor, is the last living oak of an ancient avenue felled for farmland in 1906, and its partner Gog stands dead beside it. In Chalice Well Gardens, yews grow over a spring where a yew stump dated to around 300 AD was dug up in 1961. And in St John's churchyard the Glastonbury Thorn, grafted in the 1930s, flowers in midwinter and sends a sprig to the monarch every December, the youngest of the three and the only one anyone can date.
glastonbury.meta_description: Three trees in Glastonbury: Magog, the last living oak of an ancient avenue, the Chalice Well yews, and the Holy Thorn that flowers at Christmas.
glastonbury.question_meta: Magog, the last living oak of an ancient avenue east of Glastonbury Tor, is most likely the town's oldest tree. Nobody has dated it. How to see it.
glastonbury.question_answer: Glastonbury's oldest tree is most likely Magog, the surviving one of two oaks at the foot of Stone Down, east of Glastonbury Tor, the last of an ancient avenue whose other trees were felled in 1906. Nobody has measured or dated it, and popular accounts range from about 1,000 to over 2,000 years. It stands at the edge of Wick Farm, seen free from the lane and footpath beside it, about 2.5 km east of the town centre.
glastonbury.question_context: No tree in Glastonbury carries a measured age, and the best-documented of them is the youngest. The Glastonbury Thorn in St John's churchyard was grafted by the Abbey's head gardener in the 1930s, and its story is written down to the year. Magog has no such paper trail. What is recorded is that it and its partner Gog were spared when the rest of their avenue was cut down for farmland in 1906, and that one of the felled oaks was reported at the time to have more than 2,000 rings. The Glastonbury Conservation Society notes that nobody is sure which tree is which. The living one is on the right with the Tor behind you; the other died and was scarred by an accidental candle fire in 2017. The yews of Chalice Well, a short walk away at the foot of Chalice Hill, are undated too. A yew stump found beneath the well in 1961 was dated to around 300 AD, but that tree is long dead and says nothing about the age of the living ones. If you know more about any of them, tell us.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Glastonbury?
faq.a: Most likely Magog, the surviving oak of the pair called Gog and Magog east of the Tor, the last of an ancient avenue felled in 1906. It has never been measured or dated; popular accounts range from about 1,000 to over 2,000 years.

faq.q: Can you visit Gog and Magog?
faq.a: Yes, from the lane and footpath beside them at the edge of Wick Farm, below Stone Down, about 2.5 km east of the town centre. The oaks stand on farmland, so view them from the path and stay out of the fields.

faq.q: Are there old yews at Chalice Well?
faq.a: Yes. The largest are a pair of male yews at the south end of the garden near the Holy Thorn, measured in 2006 at 8 to 10 feet round. A yew stump found beneath the well in 1961 was dated to around 300 AD. Chalice Well Gardens charge for entry.

faq.q: Why does the Glastonbury Thorn flower twice a year?
faq.a: It is Crataegus monogyna 'Biflora', a hawthorn variety that flowers once in spring like any other and again around midwinter. The trait only survives by grafting, so every Holy Thorn in Glastonbury is a cutting of the last one. Since 1929 a flowering sprig has been cut each December and sent to the reigning monarch.

wells.intro: Wells keeps its old trees inside the grounds of the Bishop's Palace, on lawns Bishop Law laid out in 1825 and 1826 where part of the medieval Great Hall had stood. Two trees there carry their own dates. A tulip tree that the Palace puts at almost 200 years old turns gold against the ruins in autumn, and two black mulberries survive from five planted in 1897, joined in 2001 by a third, a birthday present for Bishop Bickersteth. Both stand inside the paid Palace gardens, five minutes on foot from Market Place.
wells.meta_description: Old trees of Wells: a tulip tree the Bishop's Palace puts at almost 200 years and two black mulberries planted in 1897, beside the Great Hall ruins.
wells.question_meta: The tulip tree in the Bishop's Palace gardens, almost 200 years old by the Palace's account, is the oldest tree we map in Wells.
wells.question_answer: The oldest tree we map in Wells is the tulip tree in the gardens of the Bishop's Palace, which the Palace says is almost 200 years old. It stands among the specimen trees on the great lawn near the ruins of the Great Hall, inside the paid Palace gardens, about five minutes' walk from Market Place.
wells.question_context: The Palace gardens took their present shape in 1825 and 1826, when Bishop Law remodelled them as pleasure grounds and laid out a great lawn with specimen trees where the south wall of the medieval Great Hall had been. The tulip tree's age, almost two centuries by the Palace's own account, fits that date, but no record we have found names it among Bishop Law's plantings, so the age is the owner's claim rather than a documented one. The black mulberries on the same lawns are younger and better documented. Five were planted in 1897, two of them survive at about 130 years old, and a third was added in 2001 as an 80th birthday present for Bishop Bickersteth. The gardens are Grade II registered and an RHS partner garden, run by The Palace Trust with paid entry. Wells has no railway station. Buses run from Bath and Bristol to the bus station, about five minutes on foot from the Palace gate on Market Place. Neither tree has a published girth or height. If you have measured either, tell us.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Wells?
faq.a: The oldest we map is the tulip tree in the Bishop's Palace gardens, which the Palace says is almost 200 years old. It stands on the great lawn near the ruins of the Great Hall.

faq.q: How old are the mulberry trees at the Bishop's Palace?
faq.a: Two of the three black mulberries survive from five planted in 1897, so they are about 130 years old. The third was planted in 2001 as an 80th birthday present for Bishop Bickersteth.

faq.q: Do you have to pay to see the trees at the Bishop's Palace?
faq.a: Yes. Both trees stand inside the Bishop's Palace gardens, which have paid entry. Opening days and prices are on the Palace's own website.

faq.q: How do you get to the Bishop's Palace in Wells without a car?
faq.a: Wells has no railway station. Take a bus from Bath or Bristol to Wells bus station, then walk about five minutes to the Palace gate on Market Place.
